source.title: Are Gaussian Data All You Need? The Extents and Limits of Universality in High-Dimensional Generalized Linear Estimation
source.authors: L. Pesce; Florent Krzakala; Bruno Loureiro; Ludovic Stephan

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study examines test/generalization error across training-sample sizes in high-dimensional generalized linear estimation, rather than reproducing deep-network model-size or epoch sweeps.
record.gate_note: The study reports learning curves against sample complexity α=n/d, including test/generalization error curves. Its figures also compare curves with Gaussian-theory predictions; those comparisons are recorded only where they bear on the sample-size claim. Values visible only in figures are recorded as figure only. Statements and results cited from other work are not included.
record.test_reason: The study's own learning curves (Fig. 1, ridgeless ridge regression on random-feature MNIST, Fashion-MNIST and CIFAR-10) vary sample complexity α=n/d at fixed d. The authors state these show a double-descent divergence at α=1, so more samples near the threshold raise test error. The setting is linear or random-feature estimation, not deep networks, and double descent is a side observation in a paper about Gaussian universality.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, but the emphasis is off. The main conclusions are about Gaussian universality of generalized linear estimation on Gaussian mixtures. Cluster means are irrelevant when the target is uncorrelated with them. Homoscedastic mixtures match a single Gaussian, and the covariance drops out at λ=0+. Square-loss training error is strongly universal, at Δ(α−1)/α. Universality breaks under strong heteroscedasticity or teacher-data correlation, though it is restored at λ=0+ in the underparametrized regime. Double-descent universality for homoscedastic data is one consequence among several.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes high-dimensional generalized linear estimation on Gaussian mixtures and real datasets, using sample-complexity curves and asymptotic predictions; it does not use deep-network model-size or epoch sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported behavior and Gaussian agreement depend on data homoscedasticity, preprocessing, teacher/data correlation, task, noise level, and regularization.

fits_no_version.finding: The shape of the sample-wise double-descent learning curve matches the Gaussian-covariate prediction for homoscedastic data. For heteroscedastic preprocessing (raw, wavelet, orthogonal projection) the generalization curve deviates from it, while training error still matches.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The sample-wise double-descent curve is universal across data distributions only when the data are approximately homoscedastic and the target is uncorrelated with the data structure.

record.problems: The authors state that they do not provide a formal proof of Proposition 3.1. The relevant curves are presented as figures without numerical values in the supplied text; experiments report standard deviations over 30 runs.

untested.parts: No model-size sweep. The text's phrase 'number of parameters' is loose: the curves vary n at fixed d=2000.
No training-time or epoch axis; the estimators are closed-form or solver minima.
Deep networks are not tested. Whether the rise persists under finite regularization (Fig. 2) or for logistic loss is not stated.
No capacity sweep across model classes.
No effective-complexity measure is used to predict the peak location.
Noise Δ and λ∈{0.1,1,10} are varied, but the text never reports how peak height changes with noise or whether tuned λ removes the peak; no multiple peaks are reported.

missing.what: Closed-form theory for ridgeless ridge regression on a 2-cluster isotropic GMM. εgen=Δα/(α−1) for α≥1, diverging at α=1; the α<1 branch rises toward α=1. This is an analytic sample-wise peak at the interpolation threshold.
Heteroscedastic GMM ridge regression: generalization curve versus α, comparing GMM theory, simulations and Gaussian theory.

record.verdict_notes: Not an original source. Sample-wise double descent in ridgeless linear and random-feature regression is a known theoretical result, which the paper reproduces with real-data simulations; the V3 support therefore covers the shallow linear or random-feature setting only. The logistic rows are downgraded to cannot_determine because the text's double-descent statement points to the ridge panel. Proposition 3.1 is not formally proved, per the authors.

versions.untested_parts: No model-size sweep; the reported curves vary sample complexity, not model size.
The evidence is limited to sample-complexity curves for the reported generalized linear estimation tasks and data settings.
No capacity sweep across model classes.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as a predictor of peak location.
Noise levels and regularization are varied, but the study does not test whether noise or variance drives the peak, whether multiple peaks occur, or whether optimally tuned regularization removes it.
No re-counting of complexity by effective parameters.

relationships.condition: Ridgeless (λ=0+) ridge regression with a random teacher on random-feature MNIST, Fashion-MNIST and grayscale CIFAR-10, Δ∈{0.3,3}
relationships.reason: The authors say the upper panel of Fig. 1 shows a double-descent peak diverging at α=1; as n grows toward d, test error rises. Rows: the F1-*-ridge rows.
relationships.display_finding: Test error increased as n approached d and diverged at α = 1 across the studied image datasets.
